evidence: Caes. BG 7.66.1: Intereā, dum haec geruntur
terms.comment: The everyday word, in narrative and in talk alike; often with a dum-clause naming the other action (dum haec geruntur, while this was going on). In classical prose it always keeps its reference to time; the sense “nevertheless” grows out of it later (Lewis & Short).

The same as intereā (Lewis & Short), and Traupman’s word for meanwhile. After Augustus it also means “for the moment, for now” and “sometimes” (Quintilian); Cicero once has it for “nevertheless” (Att. 7.12.3, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Plaut. Men.; Ter. Eun.; Ter. Heaut. (Lewis & Short, s.v. intereā)

phrases.latin: sed fugit intereā, fugit irreparābile tempus
phrases.english: but meanwhile time is flying, flying beyond recall

phrases.latin: dum haec Taurus, intereā puer vēnerat et aula dēferbuerat tempusque esse coeperat edendī et tacendī
phrases.english: while Taurus was saying this, the boy had come back, the pot had cooled, and it was time to eat and be quiet

phrases.latin: crēscēbat interim urbs mūnītiōnibus alia atque alia appetendō loca
phrases.english: meanwhile the city kept growing, taking in one place after another with its walls

phrases.latin: Intereā, dum haec geruntur, hostium cōpiae ex Arvernīs equitēsque quī tōtī Galliae erant imperātī conveniunt.
phrases.english: Meanwhile, while this was going on, the enemy’s forces from the Arverni and the cavalry levied on the whole of Gaul gathered.
